activities.anchor: is that the listening brain is a forecasting engine
activities.caption: pair each compositional move with the game it plays
activities.name: mcExpectMatch

config.prompt: The guessing game — pair each move with what it does to the forecast:

pairs.right: violates it just enough to register as a smile
plays the same game against the beat prediction

pairs.left: a dominant seventh's tritone and minor seventh
pairs.right: create strong expectations for a specific resolution

config.why: Composers manipulate the guessing — delay, satisfy, violate — and that guessing game, not any property of the sound itself, is the emotional ride.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — when the shiver lands
activities.name: mcChillPredict

config.q: Salimpoor's PET study found dopamine release in two phases. When does the chill itself typically arrive?
choices: Just before the moment it belongs to
Long after the peak has passed
config.why: The chill frequently arrives just before the moment it belongs to — the body responding to the prediction as much as the event. Expectation theory, made physiological.

activities.caption: true or false — the earworm profile
activities.name: mcEarwormJudge

statements.s: Earworm tunes tend to a faster tempo.
statements.why: Faster tempo is part of the research profile of involuntary musical imagery.

statements.s: Their melodic contours are foreign to the listener's culture.
statements.why: The contours are common to the listener's whole listening culture — with one or two unusual interval leaps marking them as distinct.

statements.s: The Zeigarnik effect frames them: the mind keeps unfinished business active.
statements.why: A song that loops is, to the predictive brain, a pattern that keeps demanding resolution.

statements.s: An earworm is a malfunction of the memory system.
statements.why: It is the normal behaviour of a predictive, memory-hungry brain — nearly everyone reports it.

activities.anchor: The famous test case is Snowball the cockatoo
activities.caption: walk the experiment — does the bird entrain?
activities.name: mcSnowballBranch

config.root: 2009: does Snowball the cockatoo really synchronise to music, or just dance on cue? You are running the test.

choices.label: Change the music's tempo and watch whether his movements track it
choices.feedback: Exactly the 2009 design — genuine entrainment means adjusting to a beat that moves.

choices.label: Film him dancing and count the energy
choices.feedback: Motivation is not synchrony — the capacity question stays open.

tempo.text: Snowball genuinely adjusts his movements to changing tempos — the capacity can appear outside humans, but only in vocal-learning species, and nowhere near the precision of a human toddler keeping a beat.

energy.text: Enthusiasm proves nothing about the beat: dancing on cue is not beat-keeping. The decisive design changes the tempo and watches for tracking.

config.why: Beat and body co-evolved — the metrical hierarchy taught in the rhythm lessons is a description of what the motor system is doing while it listens.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — one study's reach
activities.name: mcSocietiesEstimate

config.prompt: The 2019 Harvard-led cross-cultural study behind the universality findings covered how many societies across the world?
config.why: 315 societies — every culture has music, and its social contexts recur: lullabies, dance songs, healing, love. Listeners can identify a lullaby from an unfamiliar culture above chance.
config.context: Enculturation then tunes the prediction engine to a particular tonal system within years.

activities.anchor: Plomp and Levelt mapped the curve in 1965
activities.caption: which curve matches the dissonance judgement?
activities.name: mcDissonanceTrace

config.prompt: Beating between close frequencies produces physical roughness. Which curve matches the dissonance judgement as frequency separation grows?

curves.label: roughness peaks just above unison, then decays
roughness grows without limit with separation

config.why: Plomp and Levelt's curve: beating is worst just above unison and fades as separation grows — but the same mathematics fails across cultures, because what the ear resolves and what the mind objects to are different questions.

activities.anchor: absolute pitch, the ability to name a note cold
activities.caption: place the sensitive period on the age scale
activities.name: mcPitchPlace

config.prompt: Absolute pitch is far more likely with exposure to musical training beginning at what age (years)?
config.why: Early childhood — while relative skills remain learnable for life. The prediction engine is plastic, and 'talent' is a poor first explanation.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the music-language claim
activities.name: mcLanguageSpot

config.prompt: A podcast script about music and language contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Both music and language process structured sound and build syntactic-like expectations.
Melodic intonation therapy helps stroke patients recover speech by routing language through singing and rhythm.
The circuits are identical, so any brain damage that destroys speech also destroys song.
The precise mapping between the two systems is an active frontier.
config.correction: The circuits diverge: damage can destroy speech while sparing song, and vice versa — the overlap is real but the systems are not the same machine.
config.why: Shared machinery is not identical machinery — the divergence is exactly what makes melodic intonation therapy possible.
